figure: FIGURE A.5 — Shared weights do not remove executed work
issue: In the 'Actual stop' row, a solid flow arrow enters the dashed 'pass 3' box and a second solid arrow leaves it toward 'exit'. The figure's own legend defines 'Solid arrows = flow', so the drawing asserts a flow into a node the figure simultaneously declares 'not executed'. The reader can legitimately infer that pass 3 runs and is then discarded — which is precisely the outcome the caption denies ('A true exit omits later work'). The figure's central distinction is undercut by its own arrow convention.
evidence: Rendered page 459, 'Actual stop' row: pass 1 → pass 2 → [dashed 'pass 3' box, 'not executed' beneath] → [orange 'exit' box]; both connectors appear solid. Legend: 'Dashed arrows = weight reuse; dashed box = not executed' and 'Solid arrows = flow; labeled boxes mark exit / selection'.
acceptance_test: No solid 'flow' arrow enters or leaves the not-executed box. Either the exit arrow runs directly from pass 2 and the dashed 'pass 3 (not executed)' box is placed off the flow path with no connectors, or the connectors into/out of it are dashed and the legend states that dashed connectors also mean 'skipped'. A reader tracing only the arrows cannot conclude that pass 3 executed.

figure: FIGURE A.5 — Shared weights do not remove executed work
issue: The 'not executed' annotation is set outside the dashed box, in the smallest type on the page, and is the only element preventing the misreading identified in FIG-A5-01. Its placement and size make it the first thing to be lost at print size or in a grayscale reproduction.
evidence: Rendered page 459: 'not executed' appears in small type centred beneath the dashed 'pass 3' box, outside its border, smaller than the box labels 'pass 1' / 'pass 2' / 'pass 3'.
acceptance_test: 'not executed' is set inside the dashed box as a second line at the same size as the other box labels, or the box label itself reads 'pass 3 (not executed)'.

figure: FIGURE A.5 — Shared weights do not remove executed work
issue: The legend line 'Shared core weights and iteration caches are unchanged above; omitted here for clarity' is ambiguous: 'unchanged above' can be read as 'the weights are frozen / unchanged (as in training)' rather than 'the same as in the upper diagram'. The intended meaning — that the shared weight set and the per-iteration caches drawn in the upper half are simply not repeated in the two lower paths — is not the first reading.
evidence: Rendered page 459 legend, first line: 'Shared core weights and iteration caches are unchanged above; omitted here for clarity.'
acceptance_test: The line is reworded unambiguously, e.g. 'The shared weight set and the per-iteration caches shown in the upper diagram are omitted from the two paths below for clarity.'

figure: Figures A.2, A.3, A.4, A.5 (visual semantics)
issue: Red carries three unrelated meanings across the four appendix figures: a warning/callout in A.2 ('NOT A CROSS-MODEL PERFORMANCE RANKING'), an axis/annotation device in A.4 (the vertical arrow, the 'Model intelligence ≠ system intelligence' box, the red sub-caption), and a data category in A.5 (the red-outlined 'iteration N history cache' boxes). A reader who carries the A.2/A.4 reading of red into A.5 will read the iteration caches as a warning rather than as a state category.
evidence: Rendered pages 448 (red callout box and red model names), 452 (red arrow, red sub-caption, red-outlined box), 459 (red-outlined 'iteration 1/2/3 history cache' boxes).
acceptance_test: Red is reserved for one role across the appendix (annotations/callouts), and the iteration-cache boxes in A.5 use a distinct, consistent category colour that is also distinguishable in grayscale; or the legend in A.5 states that red-outlined boxes denote per-iteration state.

issue: All four figure pages are top-aligned with roughly the bottom quarter to third of the page left blank (the figure block ends around 60–75% of the text height on each page), and on pages 451 and 452 there is an additional loose gap between the italic sub-caption and the 'FIGURE A.x' caption. The result is four pages that read as under-filled and visually unbalanced for a book of this standard.
evidence: Rendered pages 448, 451, 452, 459: content ends at approximately y=600/760 (p.448), y=600/760 (p.451), y=610/760 (p.452), y=580/760 (p.459) in a 612×792 render, with the remainder blank.
acceptance_test: Each figure page is either vertically balanced (figure + caption block optically centred in the text block) or the trailing space is eliminated by pulling the following section onto the page. The gap between the sub-caption and the figure caption is tightened to the house figure-caption spacing.

issue: The smallest annotations in all four figures — Figure A.2's italic scope sub-labels ('single-token KV cache', 'single-token inference FLOPs', 'BF16 / layer') and its two-line source line; Figure A.3's legend text and '≈YYYY' era markers; Figure A.4's 'Ch.x' references and the red sub-caption; Figure A.5's four-line legend and 'not executed' — are set in small italic grey and are the elements most likely to fall below the 8 pt print floor or to lose contrast in a grayscale proof. At 150 dpi they are legible, but legibility at 150 dpi is not the acceptance criterion.
evidence: Rendered pages 448, 451, 452, 459: the annotations listed above are visibly smaller and lighter than all other figure text; the Figure A.5 legend is four lines of small italic set below the diagram.
acceptance_test: A 100% print proof of each figure page confirms every in-figure annotation is at or above 8 pt and holds contrast in grayscale; any annotation that fails is enlarged, re-set in roman, or moved into the caption.

issue: The left-column token labels denote the step in which each token is SAMPLED, but the arrows feed directly into the 'append K/V' box with no visual indication of the one-step delay before the K/V is written. Read standalone, 'token2 / first decode → append K/V' implies token2's K/V is appended during the first decode step, which contradicts the book's own timing convention (printed p. 14: a token's K/V enters the cache on the step in which it is input, one step after it is sampled). The caption states the offset correctly, so the figure+caption unit is not wrong — but the diagram alone invites the exact misreading the book later devotes a paragraph to correcting.
evidence: Drawn labels: 'token1 / from prefill', 'token2 / first decode', 'token3 / second decode', '… tokenn / nth decode', each with an arrow into 'append K/V per layer·head'. Caption: 'written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled.' Under the book's convention, token1 (sampled at end of prefill) has its K/V written in the first decode step, and token2 (sampled in first decode) in the second decode step — i.e., every arrow crosses a step boundary that the figure does not mark.
acceptance_test: Either relabel the boxes to name the write step (e.g., 'token1 — appended in first decode') or add a short annotation on the arrow group such as 'appended one step later, when the token becomes input', so the drawn timing matches the caption without requiring the caption to rescue the diagram.

issue: The token-1 box is labelled 'from prefill' and feeds directly into 'append K/V', which can be read as saying prefill writes token 1's K/V. The prose later establishes that token 1 is sampled at the end of prefill and its K/V is written only when token 1 is processed as input in the first decode step.
evidence: Figure 1.1 shows token1 'from prefill' → append K/V. Page 14 states: 'A token's K/V therefore enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled.' The caption says 'written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled', but the diagram has no step boundary separating prefill from first decode.
acceptance_test: Either add a visible prefill/decode boundary and place token 1 on the decode side as the first decode input, or relabel token 1 as 'sampled at end of prefill; written on first decode step'. Verify a reader cannot infer that prefill appends token 1's K/V.

issue: The green consumer box is labelled 'read for attention / next token 0'. 'next token 0' is ambiguous and, on the most natural reading, wrong: token index 0 was already processed during prefill and its K/V was written then, so the cache is not read 'for token 0'. The label invites the inference that the first token is read out of the cache — the opposite of the chapter's point.
evidence: Rendered page: green box text 'read for attention' with sub-label 'next token 0'; the left column shows 'tokens / from prefill' feeding the same append path, so index 0 is already in the cache before any read occurs. The chapter's prose (printed p.14, PDF 34) states that the read happens for the token being processed, whose K/V was appended on the previous step.
acceptance_test: Replace the sub-label with an unambiguous one (e.g. 'next token to be processed' or 'token n+1'). Acceptance: no label in the figure can be read as 'the first token is read from the cache', and the label is consistent with the prefill/decode split stated on printed p.14.

issue: The caption's blanket claim — 'every token adds one K/V pair per layer per head — written when that token is next processed as input, one step after it is sampled' — is false for the prefill tokens that the figure's own left column shows ('tokens / from prefill'). Prefill tokens are never sampled; their K/V is written during the prefill pass itself. The 'one step after it is sampled' delay applies only to generated tokens.
evidence: Caption text on printed p.7 versus the figure's first left-hand box 'tokens / from prefill'. Printed p.14 (PDF 34) distinguishes the two cases: '(a) prefill populates the cache with the prefix K/V and samples the first token; ... (c) each decode step takes one input token, runs the transformer on it — which computes and appends that input token's K/V to the cache'.
acceptance_test: Qualify the caption, e.g. 'written when that token is processed as input — for a sampled token, one step after it was sampled'. Acceptance: the qualification is consistent with the prefill/decode split stated on printed p.14 and with the boxes drawn in the figure.

issue: The left column mixes number: 'tokens / from prefill' (plural, correct), 'token / first decode' (singular, correct), 'tokens / second decode' (plural, incorrect — the second decode step processes exactly one token, the first sampled token), '… token… / nth decode' (singular). Since the figure's whole claim is 'one K/V pair per token', the plural in the third box undercuts it.
evidence: Rendered page, left column box texts; printed p.14 (PDF 34): 'each decode step takes one input token'.
acceptance_test: Change 'tokens / second decode' to 'token / second decode'. Acceptance: every decode-step box in the column is singular, and the prefill box is the only plural one.

issue: The stored-K and stored-V boxes are labelled 'layer L · h₁…h₃₂', i.e. 32 heads. The book's canonical KV reference (70B, full-MHA, FP16 ≈ 2.62 MB/token; 8-bit ≈ 1.31 MB/token) implies 2.5 MiB/token = 2,621,440 B; recomputing: 2,621,440 B ÷ 2 B/element ÷ 2 (K and V) = 655,360 elements per layer, which at head_dim 128 is 64 heads per layer (e.g. 80 layers x 64 heads x 128), not 32. A reader who has internalized the canonical model will read 'h₁…h₃₂' as contradicting it.
evidence: House canonical KV values (FP16 ≈ 2.62 MB/token, 8-bit ≈ 1.31 MB/token at the 70B full-MHA reference) imply 64 KV heads at head_dim 128; the figure says h₁…h₃₂. Benign reading available: the figure is captioned '[ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]', so a non-canonical head count is not automatically an error — but the book is otherwise careful not to let illustrative figures contradict canonical values.
acceptance_test: Check the canonical head count in Ch 4, Table 4-2. If it is 64, change the label to 'h₁…h₆₄' or to a generic 'h₁…hₙ'; if the canonical is genuinely 32 heads, record that and leave the figure. Acceptance: the figure's head count equals the canonical head count, or the label is generic.

issue: The Token IDs box contains 'Integers order = position', which can be read as saying the integer token ID encodes or determines position. Token IDs are vocabulary indices; position is supplied separately by position IDs/positional encoding.
evidence: Figure 1.2: 'Token IDs / Integers / order = position'. The caption describes only 'text → tokenizer → IDs → embedding → attention → KV cache' and does not define or justify 'order = position'.
acceptance_test: Replace with 'integer vocabulary IDs; sequence order gives position' or add a separate position input. Verify the figure no longer implies that the token-ID value itself encodes position.

issue: The arrow from Embedding to Attention is labelled 'attend'. Embeddings do not attend; attention consumes the embedded token and computes Q/K/V. The label misassigns the attention operation to the embedding-to-attention transition.
evidence: Figure 1.2 shows 'Embedding' → 'attend' → 'Attention'. The Attention box itself says 'Q,K,V (this token) vs all past tokens'. The caption says 'embedding → attention', not that embedding performs attention.
acceptance_test: Relabel the arrow 'project to Q/K/V' or 'input embeddings'. Verify the word 'attend' appears only on the attention operation or the KV-cache read path, not on the embedding output.

issue: The diagram shows Attention → 'append K,V' → KV Cache, which suggests attention produces or appends K/V after computing attention. In the transformer, K/V for the current token are computed by projection before attention uses them; attention reads cached K/V and the current K/V, and the current K/V are stored for future steps.
evidence: Figure 1.2: 'Attention' box → arrow 'append K,V' → 'KV Cache'. The caption itself warns: 'The K/V are produced within every applicable layer (not after a single "attention" stage)'. The drawn causal order still places append after the Attention box.
acceptance_test: Redraw so current-token K/V are produced before or alongside attention, with attention reading past K/V from cache plus current K/V, and the append/store path clearly storing current K/V for future steps. Verify the figure no longer implies attention outputs K/V.

issue: The arrow from 'Embedding' to 'Attention' is labelled 'attend', which reads backwards: it is the attention layer that attends, not the embedding. The label is the only thing distinguishing this edge from the plain data-flow edges, and it names the wrong actor. Relatedly, the caption glosses the reverse edge as 'read (attend, the backward arrow from the KV cache back to attention)' while the figure labels that edge 'read past K,V' — the caption's parenthetical and the drawn label use different verbs for the same edge.
evidence: Rendered page: edge label 'attend' on the Embedding → Attention arrow; the reverse edge (KV Cache → Attention) is labelled 'read past K,V', which uses the correct actor-subject form. Caption: 'written (append) and read (attend, the backward arrow from the KV cache back to attention) across steps'.
acceptance_test: Relabel the Embedding → Attention edge to name the consumer ('into attention' or 'Q,K,V from') or drop the label, and make the caption's parenthetical match the drawn edge label. Acceptance: edge labels are consistent in subject-verb form across the figure and the caption quotes the drawn labels verbatim.

figure: Table 1-1 — Token throughput of the canonical workload
issue: Two defects in the same table. (i) Number formatting is inconsistent inside the value column: '~92,000' uses a thousands separator while '~368k' uses a lowercase 'k' suffix. (ii) The table is titled 'Token throughput of the canonical workload' but contains only input-token rates; the prose immediately above it also gives 'Output tokens/s: 300 x 10 = 3,000 tokens/s output', which the table omits, so the table does not carry the full throughput picture its title promises.
evidence: Rendered page: value column reads ~9,200 / ~300 / ~30x / ~92,000 / ~368k; prose above the table: 'Output tokens/s: 300 x 10 = 3,000 tokens/s output.' The arithmetic in the table is otherwise correct (9,200 x 10 = 92,000; 9,200 x 40 = 368,000; 9,200 / 300 = 30.7).
acceptance_test: Normalise the value column to one convention (e.g. '~368,000') and add an 'output tokens/s @ 10 rps' row with derivation '300 x 10 [DERIVED]', or retitle the table to 'Input-token throughput of the canonical workload'. Acceptance: the table's title matches the quantities it contains and the value column uses one number format.

issue: Caption says the pipeline is shown 'in three bands' but only ever names two of them (PREFILL top, DECODE bottom); the third band is never identified. The subsequent sentence — 'The three bands and the single PERSISTENT KV CACHE box are conceptual groupings' — then counts the KV cache box separately from the three bands, leaving the band inventory ambiguous. Visually the page shows two outlined band containers (prefill row, decode row) plus the standalone cache box, so a reader cannot reconcile 'three bands' with what is drawn or with the caption's own enumeration.
evidence: Caption, sentence 1: 'The canonical end-to-end inference pipeline, in three bands. PREFILL (top) is … DECODE (bottom) is …' (no middle band named). Caption, later: 'The three bands and the single PERSISTENT KV CACHE box are conceptual groupings for teaching, not runtime components.' Rendered figure: light rounded containers enclose only the PREFILL row and the DECODE row; the PERSISTENT KV CACHE box is a separate element between them.
acceptance_test: Caption names all three bands explicitly (e.g., 'PREFILL (top), cache-I/O (middle), DECODE (bottom)') and the band/cache sentence no longer double-counts or omits an element — or the caption is restated as 'two processing bands plus the persistent KV cache' if only two bands are intended.

issue: The caption says the pipeline is 'in three bands' and then refers to 'The three bands and the single PERSISTENT KV CACHE box'. Visually there are two process bands (PREFILL and DECODE) plus one central cache box, not three bands plus a box.
evidence: Figure 2.1 has two labelled horizontal bands, 'PREFILL' and 'DECODE', and a separate central box labelled 'PERSISTENT KV CACHE'. Caption: 'in three bands' and 'The three bands and the single PERSISTENT KV CACHE box are conceptual groupings'.
acceptance_test: Change the caption to 'two process bands plus the persistent KV-cache box' or explicitly label the cache as the third band. Verify the caption's count matches the visual grouping.

issue: The green 'initialize' path is drawn from the PREFILL band's 'first token' box into the DECODE band's 'next token' box — i.e. into the loop's OUTPUT node — instead of into the loop's INPUT node ('previous token' / 'token + position (one per step)'). As drawn, the figure asserts that the prefill's first token is the decode loop's first output, which inverts the prefill→decode handoff that this chapter exists to establish. The figure's own caption and the preceding page's prose both describe the opposite behaviour, so the drawing contradicts its own text.
evidence: Rendered page: the green line leaves the right edge of 'first token' (PREFILL band), runs down the right margin past the 'initialize' label, and terminates with a left-pointing arrowhead on the right edge of the 'next token' box in the DECODE band. The separate 'loop' arrow already runs 'next token' → 'previous token', establishing 'next token' as the loop's output node. Caption (printed p.15): 'The initial path (labelled initialize) seeds the loop with the first sampled token.' Prose (printed p.14, PDF 34): 'that first token is the input that seeds the decode loop (the green initialize path in Fig 2.1)'. Caption and prose describe a target the drawing does not implement.
acceptance_test: In the figure source, confirm the 'initialize' arrow's target node. If it targets 'next token', re-target it to 'previous token' (or to 'token + position (one per step)') and re-render. Acceptance: by inspection, the arrowhead lands on the decode band's input node, and the caption sentence 'seeds the loop with the first sampled token' is literally true of the drawing.

issue: In the PREFILL band the arrow labelled 'populate' descends from the bottom edge of the band at the boundary between the 'tokens + positions (all in parallel)' box and the 'transformer' box, so its origin is ambiguous: it can be read as the input tokens writing the cache directly, bypassing the transformer. The DECODE band has no such ambiguity — its 'append' arrow clearly rises from the transformer box. The caption says only 'it populates the persistent KV cache', without saying which stage writes the K/V.
evidence: Rendered page: the 'populate' arrow sits at x ≈ 258, coincident with the left edge of the 'transformer' box; the decode band's 'append' arrow rises from the transformer box's top-right corner. Caption: 'PREFILL (top) is the one-shot parallel pass over the whole prompt; it populates the persistent KV cache'.
acceptance_test: Move the 'populate' arrow so it originates unambiguously from the bottom edge of the 'transformer' box (and, if space allows, label it 'K/V written by each layer'). Acceptance: the prefill and decode bands use the same convention for cache writes, and no reader can infer that input tokens write the cache without passing through the transformer.

issue: The two bands use different abstractions for the same stage. PREFILL shows 'prompt' → 'tokens + positions (all in parallel)'; DECODE shows 'previous token' → 'token + position (one per step)'. The reader cannot tell whether 'previous token' is a token ID or an embedded vector, and the prefill band has no counterpart box, so the loop-carried state is not visually identified as such.
evidence: Rendered page, band contents; the 'loop' arrow returns from 'next token' to 'previous token', so 'previous token' is the loop-carried sampled token.
acceptance_test: Make the bands parallel: either label the decode band's first box 'sampled token (from prior step)' and give the prefill band the matching distinction, or drop the separate 'previous token' box and let 'token + position (one per step)' carry the loop. Acceptance: the reader can identify the loop-carried state and the embedding/position stage from the drawing alone, and the two bands use parallel vocabulary.
